summary: Defines how a SIP user agent can tell other user agents and its registrar what it can do, by adding feature parameters to the Contact header field. This allows requests to be routed to devices that can handle them, such as ones that support video.

plainLanguage.summary: A SIP device can describe what it supports, such as audio, video, or particular request types. It puts these details in Contact header parameters so registrars and other SIP elements can use them.

questions: how do sip contact header feature parameters work
how does a sip contact header describe capabilities
subtitle: How a SIP user agent describes its capabilities in Contact header parameters.

tldr.problem: SIP user agents have different capabilities and characteristics, but existing headers do not provide a general way to describe what a device can handle or what kind of device it is.
tldr.mechanism: A user agent encodes a feature set as parameters on a Contact header field. It can include them in registrations, OPTIONS responses, and messages that create or update dialogs.
tldr.outcome: Registrars and other SIP elements can use the information to select or route to a suitable device. The RFC registers an initial set of feature tags and warns that these details can be sensitive.

today: RFC 3840 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2004. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; it is paired with RFC 3841.

sections.title: Why User Agents Describe Capabilities
sections.content:
SIP user agents vary in what they can do and in the kinds of devices they represent. A caller might want a video-capable device, or an application might need to know whether a user agent can receive a MESSAGE request.

Existing headers such as Allow and Accept describe only part of a user agent's capabilities for a particular request. RFC 3840 defines a general way to describe capabilities and characteristics using Contact header parameters.
sections.plainLanguage: A caller or network service may need to choose among devices with different features. This RFC lets a SIP device describe those features in a standard place.

sections.title: Feature Tags and Feature Sets
sections.content:
A feature tag names one property, such as sip.methods. A set of tags and values describes the user agent. The RFC models a feature collection as a snapshot of what a user agent can do at a given moment.

Properties that can be present at the same time, such as audio and video, use separate tags. Different SIP methods can be values of one tag because a user agent handles one request at a time. A capability may be used in a call; a characteristic describes a fixed property of the device.
sections.plainLanguage: Each described property has a tag, such as whether a device supports audio or video. A set of tags records which features the device can handle.

sections.title: Encoding Features in Contact Parameters
sections.content:
A user agent converts its feature set into Contact header parameters. The base tags defined by the RFC appear without the leading sip.; other tags begin with a plus sign and retain their tree prefix when present.

A true Boolean feature can appear without a value. Lists of alternatives use a quoted, comma-separated value, and numeric features use a hash marker. A Contact field MUST NOT contain more than one instance of the same feature tag.
sections.plainLanguage: The Contact header uses a fixed encoding so receiving SIP elements can identify each feature tag and value. Tags defined by this RFC have a shorter form than tags added elsewhere.

sections.title: Including Capabilities in a Registration
sections.content:
A user agent registering a Contact that represents one device SHOULD include its feature set. It SHOULD NOT attach one feature set to an address-of-record that represents devices with different capabilities. A parameter can describe an address-of-record only when all devices bound to it share the same value.

A client MAY include Require: pref to ensure the registrar understands the extension. If a registration is refreshed, the user agent MUST repeat feature parameters it wants to keep active, and the registrar's successful response MUST include the parameters associated with each Contact URI.
sections.plainLanguage: A device can include its feature set when it registers. It must send the parameters again during a refresh if it wants the registrar to keep them.

sections.title: Capabilities in Dialogs and OPTIONS
sections.content:
A user agent MAY include feature parameters in Contact fields for target-refresh messages and may change them during a dialog when its capabilities change. A server receiving OPTIONS MAY include its feature parameters in the response and SHOULD reuse those from its registration.

Some feature tags overlap with SIP headers, such as sip.methods and Allow. When a header field already describes the same capability, the header field takes precedence and MUST be used instead of the feature tag.
sections.plainLanguage: A user agent can provide its capabilities in dialog messages or in an OPTIONS response. When a standard SIP header already describes the same information, that header takes precedence.

sections.title: The Initial SIP Feature Tags
sections.content:
The RFC registers tags for media types and device properties. The media tags include audio, video, text, application, data, and control. Other tags describe whether the user agent is automated, its mobility, its duplex mode, a description, its priority, methods, event packages, extensions, schemes, actor type, or whether it is a conference focus.

For example, sip.priority has the listed values 10, 20, 30, and 40 for non-urgent, normal, urgent, and emergency calls. The tags can help another element select a suitable device.
sections.plainLanguage: The initial tag set describes media support, device characteristics, and supported SIP functions. A caller can use those descriptions when choosing a device for a request.

sections.title: Privacy and Integrity of Capability Data
sections.content:
Capability parameters can reveal supported media, methods, and extensions. Other tags can reveal how a device is used, its mobility, or information about its user. Applications SHOULD protect confidentiality, integrity, and authenticity.

For registrations, the RFC recommends using a SIPS URI and digest authentication over TLS. For OPTIONS responses and dialog-initiating messages, a user agent SHOULD check with the user before revealing capability data when appropriate.
sections.plainLanguage: Capability details may reveal information about a device or its user. Applications should protect these details and verify who sent them before relying on them.
